text: The presidency of Carlos Saúl Menem lasted from July 8, 1989, to December 10, 1999, when his successor, Fernando de la Rúa, took office. It was a liberal-conservative government, typically associated with the right in Argentina. Menem won the 1989 presidential election in the first round with 48.51% of the votes and was re-elected in 1995 with 49.95% of the votes. Upon taking office, Argentina faced severe hyperinflation and recession; his first measure was a mandatory conversion of time deposits into government bonds, which worsened recession but reduced hyperinflation. Despite being a Peronist, Menem privatized several state-owned enterprises, including telephones and airlines, with YPF, the company involved in oil and gas exploration and production, being one of the most significant privatizations. As fourth economy minister, Domingo Cavallo implemented deeper neoliberal reforms, introducing the Convertibility Plan that established a one-to-one fixed exchange rate between the Argentine peso and the US dollar, while also limiting public expenditures—though this was often ignored. This policy, combined with a surge in foreign direct investment, reduced inflation from 5,000% annually in 1989 to single digits by 1993 and boosted productivity, albeit at the cost of high unemployment. Argentina's GDP, below 1973 levels when Menem began his term, increased by 35% from 1990 to 1994, and fixed investment rose by 150%. In March 1991, negotiations with Brazil led to the formation of the Mercosur customs union; on November 14 of that year, Menem addressed a joint session of the U.S. Congress, one of only three Argentine presidents to do so (the others being Raúl Alfonsín and Arturo Frondizi). His re-election in 1995 was by a large majority, though the early success of the dollar peg, which worked when the dollar was falling, gave way to economic difficulties when the dollar rose from 1995 onward, compounded by high external debt. Financial crises in Mexico (Tequila Crisis), East Asia, and Russia (1998) led to higher interest rates for Argentina, and by the end of his term, Argentina's country risk premium was 6.10 percentage points above the yield on comparable U.S. Treasuries. Menem began his presidency with a nonconfrontational approach, appointing conservative opposition members and business leaders to his cabinet. His economic recovery, driven by Cavallo’s policies, was bolstered by Justicialist Party victories in the 1991 and 1993 mid-term elections and his 1995 re-election campaign. Domestically, his administration launched programs to improve AIDS awareness, flood prevention, vaccination, and child nutrition, and introduced a Social Plan to increase spending on antipoverty initiatives, with other social programs addressing the needs of poor Argentines. These policies likely contributed to a decline in poverty during his first term. The Argentine quota law, proposed by the UCR, increased the number of women in the Argentine Congress. In 1994, after the Olivos Pact with Radical Civic Union leader Raúl Alfonsín, Menem succeeded in modifying the Constitution to allow presidential re-election. The new Constitution also introduced checks and balances, making the Mayor of Buenos Aires an elective position (previously a political appointee with significant budget control), and resulting in an opposition candidate winning the mayoral election in 1996. The president of the Central Bank and the Director of the AFIP (Federal Tax & Customs Central Agency), though political appointees, could be removed only with congressional approval. The Constitution also established an ombudsman and a board to review and propose new judicial candidates. Despite these reforms, the majority of the population and some members of the Catholic Church criticized Menem’s neoliberal policies, with unemployed workers forming the Piquetero movement and some economists labeling his financial policies as anti-liberal. These issues, along with rising crime rates, led to a defeat for his party in the 1997 mid-term elections, marking the first time his administration faltered. On December 3, 1990, Menem ordered the forceful suppression of a politically motivated uprising led by Colonel Mohamed Alí Seineldín, ending military involvement in politics. He faced strong criticism for pardoning Jorge Videla, Emilio Massera, Leopoldo Galtieri, and other leaders of the 1976–83 military dictatorship, who were convicted in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas for terrorism and the disappearance of approximately 15,000 political prisoners; he also pardoned some guerrilla leaders on grounds of national reconciliation. Nearly 50,000 people protested in Buenos Aires, and former President Raúl Alfonsín called it "the saddest day in Argentine history." Menem drastically reduced the military budget and appointed Lt. Gen. Martín Balza as Army General Chief of Staff, a figure with strong democratic convictions and a critic of the Falklands War who had defended the legitimate government in all coups and delivered the first institutional self-criticism regarding the military’s role in the 1976 coup and the subsequent terror. After the death of a conscript, Menem abolished conscription in 1994, ending military control over society. Carlos Menem Jr., the president’s son, died in a helicopter accident on March 15, 1995, at age 26; his death remains a mystery, with his parents, Zulema Yoma de Menem, suspecting murder, and ballistics expert Roberto Locles believing "Carlitos" died in an attempted assassination. Menem re-established relations with the United Kingdom, which had been suspended since the Falklands War, within months of taking office, and earned praise for resolving territorial disputes with Chile, peacefully settling over 20 border issues, including the Laguna del Desierto dispute. His tenure was most negatively affected by the Mexican peso crisis of 1995 and was marred by repeated accusations of corruption. His administration’s handling of the 1992 Israeli Embassy bombing and the 1994 AMIA Jewish community center bombing in Buenos Aires was criticized as dishonest and superficial, with suspicions that he diverted investigations from Iranian involvement to avoid confronting that power and to cover up possible links to his family friend, Alberto Kanoore Edul, a Syrian-Argentine businessman suspected of involvement in the attacks.
